description: We are Team Lunar Odyssey, a group of students passionate about technology, coding, and space exploration. We are developing MOONIX, an interactive lunar mission simulation game for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our interests include web development, lunar science, data visualization, animation, and storytelling. We welcome members interested in coding, software, space exploration, and creative problem-solving.
summary:
Moonix is an interactive lunar mission planning, simulation, and learning platform designed to help students and space enthusiasts explore potential landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole. Using NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) data and JPL Horizons calculations, Moonix allows users to compare landing locations based on sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and other mission-related factors.

Users can explore six potential landing sites, select equipment within mission budget and weight limits, assess mission readiness, and experience interactive lunar landing simulations where their decisions influence mission outcomes.

Choosing a suitable lunar landing site is challenging because missions must balance sunlight, communication, environmental conditions, and available resources. Moonix transforms complex lunar data into an engaging and accessible experience, helping users understand the scientific and practical challenges of future lunar exploration while learning to think like mission planners.
details:
Project Details :

MOONIX (Lunar Commander) is a browser-based lunar mission simulation game made for the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. The player acts as a mission commander planning a robotic landing near the Moon’s south pole.

How it works:

The player reads a mission brief and chooses one of 6 south-pole sites (Shackleton, Cabeus, Haworth, Shoemaker, Malapert Massif, de Gerlache), then picks a rim or floor landing.

The player builds the payload from 9 equipment modules under a $500M budget and 1500 kg mass limit.

In Mission Control, the player chooses a launch month and checks the sky chart, power forecast and alerts. LUNA/CAPCOM guidance helps with the GO/NO-GO decision.

Then comes the landing simulation, followed by results, a repair bay, lessons learned and a mission journal.

A “Data Sources” button shows honestly which values are NASA-based, which are game estimates, and which still need checking.

Benefits and impact: MOONIX makes real lunar science and mission trade-offs (illumination, power, mass, cost, timing) easy to understand for students and the public. It also shows why polar sites are hard and valuable.

Tools: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS (no backend, progress saved in localStorage). Python scripts (build_site_data.py, build_window_data.py) turn NASA data into game data.

Creativity: Instead of a plain data viewer, we made a decision-based game where players learn from success and failure.

Factors considered: Accuracy and honesty about data, simple UI for beginners, working in a browser without installation, and clear labelling of estimates.

SI use: AI tools were used to help write and debug code and to help with scripts and text.
